title: Tata Sons Board Reinstates Chandrasekaran for Five Years; Trusts Call Move Illegal
excerpt: The board reversed Chandrasekaran's August decision to step down, but controlling shareholder Tata Trusts says the majority vote was a "legal nullity" — and the RBI has revived the long-dodged listing question.
body:
• The Tata Sons board on Thursday voted by majority to reappoint N. Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term, reversing his August decision not to seek another term.
  • Tata Trusts, which controls about 66% of Tata Sons, called the reappointment "illegal," saying the company's articles of association require both of its nominee directors to vote in favor — and Noel Tata voted against.
  • The board also set in motion steps toward listing Tata Sons, days after the RBI rejected its bid to surrender its NBFC registration — reviving a long-dodged listing obligation.
  • An eventual listing could rank among the largest IPOs in Indian history, with a 1% stake sale estimated at ₹15,000-20,000 crore, implying a valuation near ₹20 lakh crore.

The board of Tata Sons on Thursday reversed months of succession drama, approving a third five-year term for N. Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of the Tata Group — a decision that was immediately denounced as "illegal" by the company's controlling shareholder, Tata Trusts.

The board's nomination and remuneration committee asked Chandrasekaran, 63, to reconsider his August 12 decision not to seek reappointment, according to Tata Sons' statement. He "acceded to the board's request," and the roughly three-hour meeting in Mumbai ended with a majority vote for a fresh five-year term once his current tenure expires on February 20, 2027. Chandrasekaran has led Tata Sons since February 2017.

The "legal nullity" fight

Tata Trusts rejected the outcome within hours. In a statement, the Trusts — which along with affiliated trusts control roughly 66% of Tata Sons — said the resolution was a "legal nullity" because Tata Sons' articles of association require both of the Trusts' nominee directors on the Tata Sons board to vote in favor of a chairman's appointment. Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, voted against the proposal.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2100553882946744557

The Trusts said it had filed an opinion from former Chief Justice of India D.Y. Chandrachud supporting its reading of the articles, which it said the board did not consider. Reuters' Breakingviews called the standoff a potential "lose-lose stalemate."

The dispute caps a six-month impasse. Tata Trusts had unanimously resolved last year to recommend extending Chandrasekaran's tenure, but at a February board meeting, four directors supported the extension while Noel Tata opposed it. Chandrasekaran subsequently wrote to the board saying the extension lacked unanimous support and announced in August that he would step down in February 2027.

Succession panel halted, listing revived

The vote effectively pauses the chairman-selection process the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust had initiated. In recent months the company had explored succession candidates including Tata Steel chief executive T.V. Narendran, Tata Sons group chief financial officer Saurabh Agrawal and National Stock Exchange chief executive Ashish Chauhan.

The board also resolved to "initiate steps to comply with the applicable RBI guidelines" — code for moving toward a listing of the holding company. The shift follows the Reserve Bank of India's September 11 rejection of Tata Sons' application to surrender its registration as a non-banking financial company, reviving a listing obligation that had been dodged for more than a year. Classified an "upper layer" NBFC in 2022, Tata Sons was required to list within three years; the deadline lapsed in September 2025 while its deregistration plea sat pending.

"The Board also resolved to initiate steps to comply with the applicable RBI Guidelines and will seek guidance from RBI, Tata Trusts and other stakeholders on applicable compliance requirements."

— Tata Sons, official statement

Context & Background

Tata Sons is the principal holding company of the 158-year-old Tata Group, which controls more than 30 companies including TCS, Tata Motors and Air India, with group revenue above $180 billion in 2024-25 and more than one million employees.

Friction between Chandrasekaran and Noel Tata has simmered for months over Air India's losses, a slump in Jaguar Land Rover sales, and the handling of a data leak at the group's electronics arm affecting clients Apple and Tesla. Tata Sons had even repaid over ₹21,000 crore in debt in an unsuccessful bid to escape the NBFC listing trigger.

Diaspora Angle

For diaspora investors, the stakes are direct: TCS is a top holding in Indian-American portfolios, and a Tata Sons listing could be one of the largest IPOs in Indian history — a 1% stake sale is estimated at ₹15,000-20,000 crore, implying a valuation of roughly $230 billion.

What's Next

Both the reappointment and the listing steps require approval at the company's annual general meeting. With Tata Trusts calling the vote illegal and the Shapoorji Pallonji Group — which holds about 18% — favoring a listing, the battle now moves from the boardroom to the courts and the AGM.
